items.title: Dave Brubeck — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Then the Weiss brothers said, “We’ll just take those, we’ll keep manufacturing them, we’ll call it Fantasy Records, and we’ll be partners.”

ctx.x: Then the Weiss brothers said, “We’ll just take those, we’ll keep manufacturing them, we’ll call it Fantasy Records, and we’ll be partners.” The records started really taking off. Jimmy Lyons was playing them every night on his broadcasts, so you heard them up and down the West Coast and out past the Hawaiian islands to the sailors at sea who would come into San Francisco for their leave and look me up. We had a lot of sailors at places like the Blackhawk because of Jimmy’s show. So we just kept making trio…

It was quite late at night before I heard from anybody. Then a doctor from the Tripler? Army Hospital phoned me and said, “There seemed to be some life in his limbs. He’s going to survive, but now it’s a question of how much he’s going to have use of his limbs.” But the recovery started quite remarkably fast, because he had – how many pounds?

items.title: Dave Brubeck — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The interviewer states 'I remember I met Max Weiss' and quotes him; the interviewee (Dave Brubeck) does not claim a personal relationship with Max Weiss.

ctx.x: When you’d be in the studio, and somebody would say, “Okay. Let’s go over this garbage,” it’s no way to feel good about what you were about to do. Your mood in studios – you want to have a certain dignity. The word “garbage” always stuck in my mind.

I remember I met Max Weiss. I did a long interview with him. He told me, “I’m not a jazz guy. I’ve never been a jazz guy. My philosophy is, you can’t fall in love with the product. It’s just a product.”

That’s a good description. Sol Weiss must have been an excellent recording engineer, because those old trio things are so well done. Sometimes I think with maybe one microphone. Now it takes us seven mics on the drums, balance, and all that.
